data.title: Vedanta Aluminium’s Q2FY27: Profit doubles to INR 6,187 Cr, EBITDA rises 83% YoY
data.description:
Vedanta Aluminium’s Q2FY27: Profit doubles to INR 6,187 Cr, EBITDA rises 83% YoY

  • Revenue at INR 22,066 crore, up 41% YoY
  • 2nd consecutive quarter with EBITDA exceeding INR 10,000 crore achieved
  • Highest-ever quarterly aluminium production at 649 KT, up 5% YoY & 3% QoQ
  • Net debt reduced by INR 3,090 crore QoQ, with Net Debt/EBITDA improving to 0.7x

Vedanta Aluminium Metal Limited (BSE: 544780 & NSE: VAML), India’s largest aluminium producer, announced its unaudited financial results for the quarter and half year ended 30 September 2026, delivering solid financial and operational performance.

Revenue increased to INR 22,066 crore, up 41% YoY, supported by higher volumes and improved marketing mix. EBITDA stood at INR 10,192 crore, up 83% YoY, with an EBITDA margin of ~46%. Profit after tax stood at INR 6,187 crore, more than doubling YoY with an increase of 105%.

VAML strengthened its balance sheet during the quarter, reducing net debt by INR 3,090 crore QoQ, with Net Debt/EBITDA improving to 0.7x from 0.9x in Q1FY27. The company’s credit profile was validated with India Ratings upgrading its credit rating to AA+ (Stable), alongside rating reaffirmations from ICRA and CRISIL.

Operationally, VAML achieved its highest-ever quarterly aluminium production of 649 KT, up 3% QoQ and 5% YoY. Value-added production reached a record 432 KT, increasing 31% YoY, while alumina production scaled a quarterly high of 895 KT, up 37% YoY.

Rajesh Kumar, Whole-Time Director & CEO, Vedanta Aluminium, said, “Our performance this quarter reflects the momentum in scaling VAML into a globally competitive aluminium business. The operationalisation of the second zone of BALCO’s expansion, alongside progress on securing our bauxite resources, reinforces the foundation of our integrated value chain. Our focus remains on disciplined execution, cost competitiveness, and an expanding portfolio of value-added products, enabling us to create stakeholder value and meet the growing demand for aluminium.”

Anup Agarwal, CFO, Vedanta Aluminium, said, “We sustained our earnings momentum in Q2, with revenue of INR 22,066 crore, EBITDA of INR 10,192 crore, and PAT of INR 6,187 crore. Importantly, disciplined cash generation and capital management enabled us to reduce net debt by INR 3,090 crore during Q2, improving Net Debt/EBITDA to 0.7x. With a healthy balance sheet and continued progress across growth and integration projects, we remain well positioned to fund our priorities while maintaining financial discipline.”

Sonal Choithani,
Chief Brand & Communications Officer, Vedanta
Sonal.Choithani@vedanta.co.in

data.title: Google taught the world how to search. Now it faces a revolution it can't afford to lose.
data.description:
By Christine Ji and William Gavin

Wall Street is grappling with a fundamental question: Are Google's AI Overviews bound to save search - or ruin the whole business?

Google's classic search engine is now being supplemented by new, artificial-intelligence features that are impacting revenue growth.

Google's core business, built upon ranking and indexing the open web, is facing a structural disruption as artificial intelligence changes how users navigate the internet.

When AI models like ChatGPT first became mainstream, there were concerns that consumers would query chatbots instead of turning to Google. In response to this threat, Google launched and expanded AI Overviews and AI Mode, placing AI summaries on top of traditional search results and introducing conversational search interfaces powered by its Gemini models.

But today, Google is back in the penalty box, even as these AI-powered search experiences have users asking far more questions of Google, as shown through the company's highest query growth in five years. But that couldn't keep parent company Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) from delivering third-quarter results that fell short of Wall Street's expectations, with search and advertising revenue missing the mark.

"The risk to the search business appears to have gone up recently," D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria told MarketWatch over email. The 12% search growth in the third quarter is a significant step down from the 19% growth seen at the beginning of the year, and the company warned of further pressure to search-revenue growth in the fourth quarter. Google's paid click volume has decelerated sequentially this year, falling from 13% growth in the first quarter to 8% in the third.

"Changing consumer behavior may finally be impacting advertising revenue," Luria added.

The downturn appears top of mind for investors. Alphabet lost nearly $497 billion in market capitalization on Thursday, the second-greatest one-day loss for a U.S. company on record, topped only by Nvidia's (NVDA) decline in early 2025, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Google's own AI initiatives could be driving this search slump. While the company's AI Overviews and AI Mode features have grown somewhat popular, the AI Mode in particular isn't as rife for monetization as traditional search.

Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, told investors on Wednesday that the company is seeing lower AI Mode monetization, even as it records more queries. The company wants to change that, namely by expanding ads featured in AI Mode to new countries.

Also likely weighing on growth is the popularity of Google's rivals, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT or Anthropic's (ANT) Claude. Luria pointed to growing consumer interest in agentic consumer tools like Meta Platform's (META) Muse, which can cut traditional search out of the equation entirely.

"While we are early, advertisers are likely to follow those consumers at Google's expense," Luria said.

Advertisers are indeed pursuing new strategies to get their products noticed. In a standard search campaign, a business sets a budget and bids on specific keywords that trigger text ads to appear when a user types them into the search bar. And historically, businesses also counted on getting free traffic to their sites from search engine optimization as users browsed the web. But as users lean on chatbots and AI Overviews more often, organic traffic is declining.

"Many of the ad slots are now falling below the AI Overview, so a lot of people aren't making it to that area," Conner Crowe, a fractional marketing lead, told MarketWatch.

In his role, Crowe acts as a contract marketing director for businesses. Over the past three years he's seen a broader trend of growing advertising costs on Google alongside a decrease in clicks. Among 12 local businesses whose Google ads he manages, the median business now pays more than twice as much per click as it did in summer 2023, and 11 of the 12 pay more. The median business also saw a lower click-through rate, or the percentage of people who choose to click on an ad after seeing it.

Data from marketing firm Grey Matter supports these patterns, revealing that business-to-business search clicks cost roughly 21% more from April through September 2026 than a year earlier. "From where advertisers sit, Google's search auction keeps getting more expensive as AI changes how people search," Andy Hendricks, head of search at Grey Matter, told MarketWatch.

Now, businesses are increasingly looking to get surfaced in conversations in AI Overviews or chatbots, Crowe said. While Google search treats backlinks as a core ranking signal, organic mentions on different websites such as Reddit (RDDT) are a more likely indicator of being picked up and mentioned by a chatbot, Crowe said.

For both Crowe and his clients, the "highest quality" leads are coming from AI interfaces. "Getting found in AI search is like getting a really warm referral from a good friend," Crowe added.

However, the dynamics of AI-first discovery are still uncertain. Platforms like Reddit don't want their content appearing in AI conversations without driving visitors back to their own sites, which is already turning into a problem. Reddit's referrals from search took a major hit last quarter and that trend is set to continue, according to CEO Steve Huffman, who blamed Google's "aggressive" AI push.

"The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody, as far as I know," Huffman said on a Thursday earnings call. "It's just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver, now it's not."

As new consumer habits unfold, Google is working on scaling ads within AI Overviews and AI Mode. Dan Flax, senior research analyst at Neuberger Berman, thinks that the search business can adapt to capture value from AI. Google has been experimenting with different ad formats within AI surfaces, Flax told MarketWatch, and he believes the company will be able to effectively monetize those conversational queries in the long term.

For now, Google is taking a "deliberate" approach that prioritizes user experience and engagement, Schindler said on Alphabet's earnings call.

"Google has an insane amount of users and an insane amount of habits formed, and they're in a very good position to make this transition [with AI] successfully," said Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.

-Christine Ji -William Gavin

data.title: If you really want to help your adult kids and grandkids, give them money while you're still alive
data.description:
By Richard Eisenberg

How to manage 'giving while living' without endangering your own retirement

Instead of leaving an inheritance, some retirees might want to consider making gifts while they're still alive to their adult children and grandchildren.

Amy Allen's estate plan isn't focused only on where her money will go when she dies. The Georgia mom wants to put some of it to work now.

Her 21-year-old son is getting married soon, and Allen and her husband plan to give him cash toward the purchase of a house.

"We are in a spot where we can help," she said. "If your kids are really in need, I don't think there's a reason to wait."

Although leaving bread when you're dead gets most of the attention, baby boomers, Generation X and financial advisers could look at a more helpful, immediate alternative: giving while living.

Roughly $79 trillion is expected to transfer from boomers to their heirs by 2048, according to Cerulli Associates, an asset-management research firm. You may have heard of this phenomenon, known as the "great wealth transfer."

Instead of waiting until death to leave your loved ones money, giving while living lets you help your adult children and grandchildren financially now, or in the near future, when they could truly use the assistance. Any money left over can become an inheritance one day.

Yet in a 2024 Charles Schwab survey, 45% of boomers with $1 million or more in investible assets said they want to enjoy their money for themselves while they're still alive. That could disappoint many millennial and Gen Z adult kids. A recent Kiplinger-Morning Consult survey found nearly twice as many adult children preferred that their parents help them financially now rather than giving them a larger inheritance later.

Giving while living

There are plenty of reasons so many people could use immediate, tax-free gifts from their boomer and Gen X parents. The median net worth for people in their 30s is $28,616, according to Empower, and their median liquid savings is $7,000, according to the Federal Reserve. Steep housing prices and mortgage rates have put homes out of reach for many young adults. College tuition is also through the roof and expected to continue rising, putting some 43 million Americans in debt for an education.

Giving while living might help your adult children to afford a home, be it a house or an apartment, or to stay afloat after a job loss. Putting money into a 529 college savings fund for a grandchild could make higher education attainable for them.

"Giving while living can be very meaningful in the moment," said Laura Varas, CEO of Hearts & Wallets, a wealth-management market research firm. "It's very hard for people in their 20s and 30s to make ends meet."

Varas, a Gen X-er, knows this personally. She just gave her daughter roughly $5,000 toward a down payment on a London apartment. "For her, being able to be in a roach-free, slightly-bigger-than-a-matchbox apartment has a lot of utility," Varas said. "I'm sure she's very grateful for it, and it makes me feel good."

That's how my wife and I see it, too. We expect to help one of our sons with a down payment on a home in Los Angeles once he has enough savings for the monthly payments. We've also been regularly contributing to 529 plans for our other son's two young children, which we plan to continue.

Roughly 27% of boomers financially support their children, up from 12% in 2015, according to Hearts & Wallets. Some boomer and Gen X parents and grandparents, however, are hesitant, fearing doing this could endanger their own financial security if they run into steep healthcare or long-term-care costs.

If you're one of them, or you're unsure about the best ways to lend a hand to your adult kids or grandkids, here's what experts suggest.

Determine whether you can afford to give

Running out of money is a common fear among current retirees and near-retirees. "We often hear, 'I don't want to jeopardize my retirement,'" said Jessica Ray, a Washington, D.C., senior growth adviser with Brighton Jones, a wealth-management firm.

Sandy Goldman, author of "The New 65: Rewiring, Not Retiring" and founder of the "65Nation" newsletter, calls this everyone's biggest fear about giving while living.

"Basically, you've got to come to the conclusion that you have X dollars to live on and that you're going to bequeath, so what is the amount you could live without?" he said. "You just have to make that leap of faith to feel you can cover the worst-case scenarios and still be able to share what you have now."

To ease nerves about giving large amounts of money while you're still alive, dig into the numbers. Create a budget for current and anticipated expenses, including your financial goals and intended care plan. Next, estimate a higher-than-anticipated inflation rate and a lower-than-expected stock-market performance. "Then we see where we end up," said Ray of Brighton Jones.

When people tell Ray they're not ready, or able, to give money to their adult children or grandchildren, she suggests they read the bestseller "Die With Zero: Getting All You Can From Your Money and Your Life" by Bill Perkins, a multimillionaire hedge-fund manager. Perkins, 57, is a big proponent of giving adult kids money when it can have "a maximum impact in their life," rather than only after the parents die.

If you also expect to leave money to your children in a will or trust, you might want to explain to them that your assistance now will reduce their inheritance later. That's what Georgia retiree Mel McGill told his kids. "They understood that my help was not free money," he said.

Decide when to do your giving

Have conversations with your adult children about what you're thinking, what would be helpful to them and when.

Put some of the responsibility on your kids, Ray said. "Have them make a budget and quantify what they need. Then review it with them, and make sure you feel good about the plan," she said.

Be sure you know your child's full financial situation so you can avoid making an unnecessary gift. For example, Ray said, before contributing to a grandchild's 529, check to see whether other family members or relatives are taking care of that. If so, you might want to help out another way.

The best times to assist your children financially may come at different points in their lives.

Two years ago, when one of McGill's sons sold his home and couldn't afford to buy and make mortgage payments on another one because prices had risen so much, McGill let him move into one of his own rental properties and pay rent. More recently, when McGill's daughter needed money for a down payment on a place whose monthly payments she could manage herself, dad obliged.

Choose how you want to give

You might prefer to loan money and receive regular payments, rather than making a no-strings gift. If the loan is over $10,000, be sure to charge at least the IRS's applicable federal rate: currently 4.25% for up to three years, 4.61% for three- to nine-year loans and 5.22% for loans over nine years.

If you have more than one child, don't confuse equality with fairness. It's only human for a parent to want to help one child when he or she loses a job while also worrying about being unfair to a sibling. "I think it's important to feel like you can help whoever needs the most amount of help and know things will self-adjust over time," Ray said.

If you're considering giving a child $20,000 or so, you may want to trim your generosity to $19,000 in 2026. That way, your gift will be below the threshold reducing your federal estate-tax exemption. (A married couple can give up to $38,000 to an individual in 2026.) The unified lifetime exemption is $15 million per individual in 2026.

Financial advisers could do a better job helping people incorporate giving while living, Varas said. According to her firm's research, less than a third of advisers whose clients have adult children talk with them about this type of assistance.

If you have a financial adviser, you may want to arrange a meeting that includes your adult child to discuss specifics about making gifts wisely.

Once you start giving while living, you'll likely find it's a wonderful way to leave a legacy. "It's more blessed to give than receive," said Allen. "You can't put a price on it."

-Richard Eisenberg

data.title: The stock market's front-runners stumbled in October. Here's where the smart money is moving now.
data.description:
By Christine Idzelis

Investors are shifting money into stocks with defensive and high-quality characteristics

Investors were spooked by the tech selloff in October.

U.S. stocks saw a strong reversal in fortunes in October, as worries about dwindling free cash flows and rising borrowing costs threw a wrench into the artificial-intelligence trade.

Tech stocks were punished, with the S&P 500's information-technology sector XX:SP500.45 snapping back-to-back monthly gains to drop 6.8% for its worst month since March 2025, FactSet data showed. Investors - spooked by fears that companies may not deliver the payoff they had expected from AI despite continuing to pour money into building data centers - leaned into traditionally more defensive parts of the equities market. They're also eyeing high-quality stocks to help mitigate sudden tech blows.

Friday's clobbering of the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF SPMO, which tracks stocks in the U.S. large-cap equities index that have a high momentum score and whose portfolio is heavily weighted toward tech, left the exchange-traded fund with a 10.1% loss in October. The iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF MTUM, which seeks to capture market trends by investing in U.S. stocks with strong recent performance, booked a similar drop of 10.5% in October, according to FactSet data.

"We're buying quality," said Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist at LPL Financial, in a phone interview. "When you buy quality products, you are getting a little bit of a value tilt, and you're getting a little bit of underweight to the AI trade, particularly to the lower-quality segment of the AI trade."

Marta Norton, Empower's chief investment strategist, also pointed to stocks with quality characteristics as desirable in the current environment, citing their "lower levels of debt, consistent earnings streams and a measure of growth embedded in the revenue profile."

While tech's struggles in October dragged the S&P 500 SPX and Nasdaq Composite Index COMP into the red, high-quality stocks generally appeared to hold up amid the AI-related carnage.

Take the iShares MSCI USA Quality Factor ETF QUAL, which aims to invest in U.S. stocks with stable earnings and low debt. The fund ended October with a slight 0.1% gain, according to FactSet data. By contrast, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.3% in October, cementing its worst monthly performance since March 2025, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

As the AI trade's recent comeback violently reversed in October, investors have sought shelter in Treasury bonds while also taking cover in traditionally defensive stock-market sectors, like healthcare XX:SP500.35, utilities XX:SP500.55 and consumer staples XX:SP500.30.

The State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF XLP, the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF XLU and the State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF XLV all saw enormous rallies in October.

The consumer staples ETF, whose top three holdings as of Thursday included Walmart (WMT), Costco Wholesale (COST) and Procter & Gamble Co. (PG), soared 10.9% in October. That huge gain left the State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF with its largest monthly gain ever since it began trading in 1998, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

While consumers still appear to be spending despite sticky inflation, purchases of discretionary items risk falling off if the stock market experiences a big drawdown that makes investors worried about a drop in their wealth, Russell Price, chief economist at Ameriprise Financial, told MarketWatch by phone. But consumer staples tend to fare relatively well when the economy slows, as people continue to shop for items like soap, toothpaste and shampoo.

Consumer staples tend to be "a safer place to be within the equity market," said Empower's Norton, "as there's just not a whole lot of earnings volatility there." But she cautioned that, at this point, the consumer-staples sector appears "overvalued" following its recent surge.

The S&P 500's consumer-staples sector has gained almost 16% this year after its October spike, according to FactSet data.

Still, the index's tech sector has seen an even bigger gain so far in 2026 - around 19% - despite fears over the AI trade as chip stocks sold off in October.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index SOX plunged more than 15% in October, with Intel's shares (INTC) plummeting 28.6% on Friday alone after the company's quarterly earnings report disappointed investors.

Big Tech stocks also fell Friday, as investors digested Amazon.com's (AMZN) quarterly earning results. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF MAGS - whose holdings include seven Big Tech stocks including Amazon, Nvidia (NVDA), Google parent Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), Facebook parent Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) - dropped 4.5% in October, according to FactSet.

Hyperscalers in that group are at the center of "the AI storm." But they have appreciated by less than hot chip stocks, making them less vulnerable to a pullback, according to Norton.

The market seems to be "calling the wrestling match after the first takedown instead of waiting to see how it plays out over time," she said. "I don't think we know who the winners and losers are because we don't know exactly how customers and enterprises are going to change their behavior and interact with AI."

While the U.S. equities market's stumble in October was largely triggered by a selloff in the technology sector and Big Tech due to AI anxiety, an equal-weight version of the S&P 500 pulled off a gain as the average stock appeared to do well week after week.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF RSP rallied almost 5% in October, ending Friday with a fourth straight week of gains, according to FactSet data. By contrast, the S&P 500 booked a monthly loss of 0.9%, falling for a third straight week to reduce its 2026 gain to 10.7%, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

-Christine Idzelis

data.title: Alligator Bioscience Signs Agreement To Sell Mitazalimab to Biossil
data.description:
LUND, SE / ACCESS Newswire / October 31, 2026 / Alligator Bioscience (STO:ATORX)(Nasdaq Stockholm:ATORX), a biotechnology company whose principal asset is a financial interest in the HER2-targeting antibody program HLX22, today announced that it has signed an agreement to sell all rights and assets related to the CD40 agonist antibody mitazalimab to Biossil Inc. ("Biossil"). Alligator will receive USD 0.75 million upfront and is eligible for up to USD 108 million in milestone payments, as well as royalties on future sales.

Under the agreement, Biossil acquires worldwide rights to mitazalimab, including its derivatives, for all indications and uses, including patents, clinical and regulatory data, know-how, manufacturing materials and drug inventory. From closing, Biossil will be responsible for all further development, manufacturing and patent costs, and has committed to develop mitazalimab.

As consideration, Alligator will be paid USD 0.75 million as an upfront payment. The milestone payments consist of up to USD 3 million in total upon first regulatory approval in the US and EU.

In addition, Alligator is eligible for up to USD 105 million linked to worldwide net sales, and mid-single-digit royalty on worldwide net sales, capped at USD 250 million in total. All payments other than the upfront payment are contingent on future events and there can be no assurance that they will be received.

If Biossil sells or licenses mitazalimab to a third party within two years of the signing of the agreement, Alligator will receive a share of the proceeds from such transaction.

Alligator believes the transaction provides an attractive balance between near-term value realization and potential future upside through milestone and/or royalty-based consideration.

Completion of the transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including the transfer of assets and documentation and receipt of required third-party consents. Closing is expected within 30 days of signing. The proceeds are expected to extend Alligator's financial runway and support the execution of its strategic objectives.

The sale of mitazalimab is in line with Alligator's previously communicated strategy to focus on its economic interest in HLX22, and ends Alligator's costs for maintaining the mitazalimab program and related IP portfolio from closing.

"Mitazalimab has shown promising data in pancreatic cancer, and with this agreement it gets an owner that can take mitazalimab forward towards registrational trials. Importantly, Alligator, and thus our shareholders, keep a stake in the future value of the program," said Søren Bregenholt, CEO of Alligator Bioscience.

"We thank Alligator for entrusting Biossil with continued development of mitazalimab," said Alexander Mosa, CSO & Chair of Biossil. "Patients and investigators have invested time and hope in this therapy, which we will reciprocate with rigor and focus."

For further information, please contact:

Søren Bregenholt, CEO
E-mail: soren.bregenholt@alligatorbioscience.com
Phone: +46 (0) 46 540 82 00

Johan Giléus, CFO
E-mail: johan.gileus@alligatorbioscience.com
Phone: +46 (0) 46 540 82 00

This information is information that Alligator Bioscience is obliged to make public pursuant to the EU Market Abuse Regulation. The information was submitted for publication, through the agency of the contact persons set out above, at 2026-10-31 08:15 CET.

About Alligator Bioscience
Alligator is a biotechnology company that has historically focused on tumor-directed immuno-oncology. Following a strategic refocus, Alligator is prioritizing the value of its economic interest in HLX22, an anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody being developed by Shanghai Henlius Biotech Inc., from which Alligator is entitled to a share of revenues without incurring development costs. Alligator has discontinued further internal development of mitazalimab and in October 2026 agreed to sell the asset to Biossil Inc.

Alligator is listed on Nasdaq Stockholm (ATORX) and headquartered in Lund, Sweden.

For more information, please visit alligatorbioscience.com.

About Biossil
Biossil is an AI-native drug development company advancing a pipeline of late-stage, first-in-class candidates for heterogeneous and life-threatening diseases. With teams in Toronto and Boston, and partnerships with leading academic medical centers and research hospitals, Biossil integrates proprietary AI with deep clinical and translational expertise to advance promising clinical-stage assets.

data.title: This Halloween, are full-size candy bars a better deal than fun-sized ones?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

Several influencers claim you can save money and be the coolest house on the block with bigger candy this year. Let's see how that adds up.

As the cost of Halloween candy climbs, does it make more sense to hand out full-size chocolate bars this year?

Soaring candy prices have many Americans looking to scare up some extra value during what has been an already expensive year. And one claim is going viral this spooky season: that giving out full-sized candy bars to Halloween trick-or-treaters makes more financial sense than bagging the smaller "fun size" sweets.

The logic, according to a handful of TikTok creators, is that the price for buying full-sized bars in bulk at discount giants like Costco and Sam's Club, and the seasonal mixed bags of mini candies, are about the same this year.

"You should be handing out full-size candy bars," says a TikTok creator by the username Z. Hartleben in a clip that's drawn almost 14,000 likes and hundreds of comments. The argument is that the variety packs of 120 mini Halloween candies run between $18 and $20 - but they don't necessarily serve 100 kids, because trick-or-treaters tend to grab handfuls. So a big bag of mini candies may only satisfy 30 kids, by her reasoning.

But they'll only take one full-size bar apiece, she argues. So scoring a $20 pack of 30 full-size Hershey bars (according to her Costco receipt) delivers more bar for the buck, in her opinion. "The math just makes a little more sense with full-size bars," she says.

Another TikTok from creator, Somer Agnor, agrees. "The craziest part about the full size candy bars is that it's really not that much more expensive than getting one of those variety packs of candies," she says in a video that's drawn over 900 likes. She also bought a box of full-size Hersey bars in bulk, paying, she says, $30 for 30 chocolates.

Still other posts feature shoppers sharing where they've scored full-sized bars on sale for a little over $20.

Halloween spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion this year, according to the National Retail Federation, with $4.1 billion alone being spent on candy.

And candy prices are up 15.3% over last year, according to data from Groundwork Collaborative and Century Foundation, which also looked at how individual candy brands have become more expensive. The Hershey (HSY) variety pack, which includes Kit-Kat bars and Reese's peanut-butter cups, is up 19.03% from last year, according to Groundwork Collaborative data, and the Mondelez (MDLZ) gummy-candy variety pack, which includes Swedish Fish and Sour Patch Kids, is up 13.16%.

As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, the Associated Press reported, citing government data. Halloween candy sales have also gotten off to a slower start this year as Americans grapple with higher prices, the same report noted, with sales down 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared with the same period last year.

So the idea of going all-in on full-size bars is intriguing: You can save money and be the coolest house on the block?

Does that logic actually add up?

It all hinges on whether you're able to get those big bars at a big discount - and you may have missed the window. As of Friday morning - the day before Halloween - Costco (COST) was still advertising the 30-pack of full-sized Hershey bars for about $20 - if you're a member and picking them up in-store. Ordering online for delivery could set you back $30 or more, however. But at Target (TGT), a pack of 18 full-sized Hershey bars was $32.49 online as of Thursday - which was still twice the price of a 25-ounce "party bag," which can contain up to 70 fun-size pieces of candy, at $16.99. At Walmart (WMT), the 18-pack of full-sized Hershey bars was $24.88 online on Friday, while the 25-ounce fun-sized bag was $13.99 - still a good $10 less.

So the cheaper option in most cases is to buy the bag of fun-sized treats - and encourage kids not to be greedy in how much they grab.

Either way, expect to spend more money on Halloween candy this year.

Why candy prices are up

Some materials involved in producing candy - notably cocoa - are more expensive than they were a few years ago.

"Cocoa costs have soared over the past several years, and raising prices is one way manufacturers offset those pressures," says Erin Lash, the director of community equity research at Morningstar.

In 2022, cocoa (CC00) costs ranged from $2,200 to $2,550 per metric ton, according to data from the International Cocoa Organization. Prices peaked in January 2025 at $10,750, and, while they've come down from that high, they were sitting around $5,600 as of Friday morning.

Elizabeth Pancotti, a vice president of policy at Groundwork Collaborative, notes that rising oil prices (CL00) (BRN00) have also played a part.

"Because the war in Iran is driving up oil cost, and plastic is made of oil, the cost of packaging has gone up, and there is a lot more packaging for Halloween candy because Halloween candy has to be individually wrapped," she says.

But Pancotti also notes that both sugar and corn syrup costs are lower this year than they were last year and in 2024, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, making some candy more affordable to produce. She suggests that company profit margins are playing a role in pushing up prices.

"Instead of passing those savings on to consumers and lowering their prices, they are keeping them high and expanding their profit margins," says Pancotti.

Neither Hershey nor Mondelez was immediately available for comment.

The bottom line: If you're planning to hand out candy this Halloween, you'll be paying more - no matter how big your chocolate bars are.

-Aditi Shrikant

data.title: White Paper Outlining Strategies to Address Rural AI Skills Gaps and Support Workforce Retention Published by the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies
data.description:
White Paper Outlining Strategies to Address Rural AI Skills Gaps and Support Workforce Retention Published by the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies

White Paper Outlining Strategies to Address Rural AI Skills Gaps and Support Workforce Retention Published by the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies

PR Newswire

PHOENIX, Oct. 31, 2026

Author Dr. Stella Smith draws on Career Optimism Index® study to explore informal AI adoption, limited employer resources and career pathway challenges facing rural workers and businesses.

PHOENIX, Oct. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies has published a new white paper, "Bridging the Rural AI Skills Gap: Overcoming Informal Adoption, Resource Constraints, and Career Pathway Traps," by Stella Smith, Ph.D., associate university research chair for the Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR). Drawing on findings from the University of Phoenix Career Institute® 2026 Career Optimism Index® study and published workforce research, the paper examines how independent artificial intelligence (AI) skill development, limited organizational resources and unclear career pathways can create workforce challenges for rural employers and communities.

In the white paper, Smith explores how a growing disconnect between workers developing AI capabilities and employers' readiness to support and recognize those skills may be particularly consequential in rural labor markets, where smaller businesses, limited access to formal training and fewer local career opportunities can complicate workforce development and increase concerns about retaining AI-skilled talent.

"Rural workers may already be building valuable AI capabilities on their own, but employers need systems that help recognize, develop and apply those skills," said Smith. "For smaller communities, the challenge is not simply keeping pace with technology. It is creating accessible training, clear career pathways and organizational support so that emerging capabilities can contribute to both individual career growth and local economic resilience."

How is informal AI adoption affecting workforce development?

In the white paper, Smith draws on findings from the 2026 Career Optimism Index® national study examining workers' career perceptions and employers' workforce challenges, highlighting several trends shaping AI skills development and organizational readiness:

  • 50% of workers report learning to use AI independently, without formal employer training.
  • 60% of workers say they want more guidance in learning AI tools.
  • 62% of employers say employees are developing AI skills faster than their organizations can adapt.
  • 48% of employers are concerned about their ability to retain AI-fluent talent.

Applying these national workforce findings to rural economic conditions, where employers may have fewer resources to provide structured AI training or establish formal processes for evaluating emerging skills, the paper also examines potential risks associated with informal, uncoordinated AI adoption, including inconsistent workplace practices, data governance concerns and missed opportunities to recognize employees' developing capabilities.

Why do rural communities face distinct AI workforce challenges?

Rural labor markets often depend on small and medium-sized businesses, agricultural enterprises, healthcare organizations and public institutions that may lack dedicated training resources or the infrastructure needed to support organization-wide AI adoption. Smith's analysis identifies three interconnected challenges: reliance on self-directed AI learning, organizational constraints on workforce development and limited local career pathways that recognize newly acquired skills.

Without structured opportunities to apply and develop these capabilities, AI-fluent rural workers may increasingly consider employment with organizations offering clearer professional development opportunities, including remote positions outside their local communities.

The paper suggests that addressing these challenges requires regional approaches that connect workforce education, employer needs and career development.

What strategies can help rural employers close AI skills gaps?

Smith proposes a three-part roadmap to help rural employers, educational institutions and workforce development organizations support responsible AI adoption and skills development:

  • Build regional education and industry collaborations. Encourage employers, higher education institutions and workforce organizations to pool training resources and develop accessible, industry-aligned learning opportunities, including stackable credentials that document AI competencies.
  • Establish transparent skills assessment and career pathways. Identify existing AI capabilities, clarify expectations for AI use and connect skills development to defined opportunities for employees to apply their knowledge and pursue professional growth.
  • Equip managers to support AI skills development. Prepare supervisors to identify appropriate AI applications, evaluate AI-assisted work and guide employees in developing and applying new capabilities.

The roadmap emphasizes moving beyond informal experimentation toward coordinated workforce development practices that support both organizational needs and employees' career goals.

Smith concludes that strengthening AI skills development in rural communities will require collaboration among employers, education providers and regional leaders. By aligning training, skills recognition and career development, these stakeholders can help rural organizations make better use of emerging AI capabilities while supporting local workforce resilience.

The full white paper is available on the Research Hub.

About the author
Smith is the associate university research chair for CEITR and an associate faculty member in the College of Doctoral Studies at the University of Phoenix whose work focuses on organizational wellness, access to opportunity and the implications of technological infrastructure on workforce outcomes. Her research integrates applied data with strategic insights to help leaders implement initiatives that strengthen employee well-being and organizational performance. Smith earned her doctorate in educational administration from The University of Texas at Austin.

About University of Phoenix
University of Phoenix is Built for Real Life. 50 Years Strong. The University innovates to help working adults enhance their careers and develop skills in a rapidly changing world through flexible online learning, relevant courses, academic AI pillars, and skills-mapped curriculum for associate, bachelor's and master's degree programs. Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for Life® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu. 

About the College of Doctoral Studies
University of Phoenix's College of Doctoral Studies focuses on today's challenging business and organizational needs, from addressing critical social issues to developing solutions to accelerate community building and industry growth. The College's research program is built around the Scholar, Practitioner, Leader Model which puts students in the center of the Doctoral Education Ecosystem® with experts, resources and tools to help prepare them to be a leader in their organization, industry and community. Through this program, students and researchers work with organizations to conduct research that can be applied in the workplace in real time.

data.title: These 10 megadonors have spent a total of $1 billion on the midterm elections
data.description:
By Victor Reklaitis

They've helped turn this year's midterms into 'the most expensive election cycle on record'

How big is the spending on the midterm elections? It's setting records.

Top individual megadonors in this year's midterm elections are mostly favoring Republican candidates, delivering a big boost to the GOP's bid to keep its grip on the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate.

"In many places, the Democratic candidates have outraised the Republican candidates, and Republican megadonors are one reason that a GOP-aligned super PAC calvary has been able to come in and help keep a lot of those races competitive - in terms of the ads that are being aired, in terms of what's being done to advance messages," said Michael Beckel, director of the money-in-politics reform program at Issue One, an advocacy group.

"It is just some really jaw-dropping, astonishing amounts of money that some of these top donors have pumped into the 2026 midterms," he added.

The table below, based on data from watchdog group OpenSecrets, shows the 10 biggest individual contributors to super PACs and other outside groups for the current election cycle. Super PACs are political action committees that can receive and spend unlimited amounts of money. Just two of these top 10 donors gave mostly to Democratic or left-leaning outside groups.

The top donors to outside groups 

 
Rank             Donor name            Affiliated enterprise  Home state  Total contributions  % to Democratic/left-leaning  % to Republican/right-leaning 
1                Musk, Elon                    SpaceX, Tesla          TX         $445,457,890                             0                            100 
2          Uihlein, Richard                            Uline          IL         $141,963,415                             0                            100 
3                Yass, Jeff  Susquehanna International Group          PA         $109,000,000                             0                            100 
4        Bloomberg, Michael                     Bloomberg LP          NY          $82,878,998                          97.6                              0 
5           Adelson, Miriam                   Adelson Clinic          NV          $66,097,500                           0.1                           99.9 
6          Andreessen, Marc              Andreessen Horowitz          CA          $55,780,000                           0.1                           12.4 
         Horowitz, Benjamin              Andreessen Horowitz          CA          $55,780,000                           0.1                           12.4 
8              Singer, Paul               Elliott Management          FL          $48,712,400                             0                           94.7 
9             Hoffman, Reid                Greylock Partners          WA          $38,468,724                           100                              0 
10      Schwarzman, Stephen                 Blackstone Group          NY          $35,435,400                             0                            100

The total amount of money contributed by these 10 contributors, who all have been big spenders in past election cycles, is $1.08 billion, according to OpenSecrets data. SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) CEO Elon Musk accounts for nearly half of that outlay.

These donations are helping this year's midterms set spending records. AdImpact, an ad-tracking company, said this week that it projects advertising spending of $11.6 billion for the 2026 election cycle, topping the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential election to rank as the "the most expensive election cycle on record." (Adjusting for inflation, the 2024 outlay would be around $12 billion.)

An important factor behind the elevated spending is the growing number of competitive races, according to Issue One's Beckel.

"As the political climate has deteriorated for national Republicans and for President Trump's popularity, a lot of seats have been viewed as much more competitive than they were just a few months ago or at the beginning of the cycle," Beckel told MarketWatch. "When you've got competitive races, you've got a lot of money flowing into competitive races, and I think that perfect storm has helped enable a lot of new records to be shattered this election cycle."

Musk has been vocal about his reasons for supporting Republican candidates, writing in a social-media post this week that his "biggest concern" is that Democrats winning the House, Senate and presidency in the 2028 election would lead to changes such as statehood for the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, as well as citizenship for "everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority."

"This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word," said Musk, who is the world's richest man, with an estimated net worth of around $874 billion. "All that is needed to ensure this doesn't happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one."

Democrats have a 94% chance of winning the House and a 71% likelihood of capturing the Senate, according to prediction market Kalshi.

-Victor Reklaitis

Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. and ICP DAS Showcase iTLC Intelligent Traffic Control Solutions at APTA 2026 in Chicago

Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. and ICP DAS Showcase iTLC Intelligent Traffic Control Solutions at APTA 2026 in Chicago

PR Newswire

CHICAGO, Oct. 31, 2026

Advancing smart intersection technologies and expanding international market opportunities through strategic collaboration

CHICAGO, Oct. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Towards Buddha Co., Ltd., an overseas distributor of the iTLC Intelligent Traffic Control System, joined its technology partner ICP DAS at APTA 2026 TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago, USA, to showcase the iTLC-9000 Series and its applications in intelligent traffic management.

The exhibition highlighted innovative traffic control technologies designed to support reliable, secure, and integrated smart intersection operations, while providing opportunities to connect with international transportation professionals and explore emerging market needs.

Innovative Traffic Control Solutions

Under the theme "Innovative Traffic Control System," the exhibition featured the iTLC-9000 Series, highlighting four key capabilities: modular and redundant design, secure networking, traffic signal integration, and active alert systems.

These technologies are designed to support system reliability, communication security, and efficient traffic infrastructure management, addressing the evolving requirements of modern intelligent transportation systems.

As cities worldwide continue to modernize transportation infrastructure, integrated and adaptable traffic control solutions are becoming increasingly important for smart intersection development.

Strengthening International Market Connections

As an overseas distributor of iTLC solutions, Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. plays an important role in connecting traffic control technologies with international markets.

During APTA 2026, Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. and ICP DAS engaged with transportation professionals, system integrators, and industry representatives to introduce iTLC technologies, exchange industry insights, and explore potential business opportunities.

"APTA 2026 provided a valuable platform to connect with the global transportation industry," said a representative of Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. "Together with ICP DAS, we look forward to expanding international awareness of iTLC solutions and developing new opportunities in intelligent traffic control."

Looking Ahead

Building on its participation at APTA 2026, Towards Buddha Co., Ltd. will continue collaborating with ICP DAS to promote iTLC solutions, strengthen international partnerships, and explore new opportunities in the global intelligent transportation market.
